$comment: AI system manifest and lifecycle identity. Standard 1 requires the manifest; Standard 3 governs the policy that selects rules. Model identity is declared here in Phase 1 because the manifest is the only place it is declared at all; the broader lineage story is Standard 30 and arrives with Phase 2. Standard 8 adds the safety requirements record and safety case rules (lifecycle.safety-*): no safety. namespace is reserved, and these are system-level documents maintained across the lifecycle, so they sit here rather than in misuse. (item 9) or oversight. (items 10 and 11).

rules.title: The AI system declares itself in a manifest
rules.description: A committed ai-system.yml declares the system's models, prompts, tools, data sources, autonomy tier and lifecycle stage.
rules.rationale: Every other rule in this pack asks a question about a declared thing. Without a manifest there is nothing to ask about, and an evaluator that proceeds anyway is guessing at the system's shape from filenames.
rules.remediation: Add ai-system.yml at the repository root declaring the system.
rules.$assuranceNote: File presence is fully decidable. This asserts a file exists; it asserts nothing about whether its contents are true.

rules.title: The manifest conforms to its schema
rules.rationale: A manifest that does not parse or does not conform cannot be read by any other check, so every rule that depends on it silently degrades to unevaluated.
rules.remediation: Correct the manifest against the schema; the validator names each violation.
rules.$assuranceNote: Schema conformance is fully decidable. A conforming manifest may still describe a system that does not exist.

rules.title: The manifest is written, not generated and left
rules.description: The manifest carries no scaffold marker and no placeholder-only sections.
rules.rationale: A bootstrap that writes a manifest, and an evaluator that then accepts it, means the framework wrote its own evidence. Scaffolding is not evidence.
rules.remediation: Replace the generated placeholders with the system's actual declarations, then remove the scaffold marker.
rules.$assuranceNote: Two independent signals — an explicit marker and section substance — either of which alone is defeatable. A document passing both may still be wrong; it is merely not a template.

rules.title: Declared models are pinned, not floating aliases
rules.description: Every model identifier the manifest declares names a specific version rather than a moving alias.
rules.rationale: A floating alias means the system under evaluation is not the system that ships. Every evaluation result, every approval and every attestation silently describes a different model the moment the provider re-points the alias.
rules.remediation: Replace the alias with the dated or versioned model identifier the provider documents.
rules.$assuranceNote: Recognises alias shapes from a maintained list. A provider may retire an alias form or re-point a pinned-looking id server-side; this cannot see that. Because the check covers less than the rule, a clean result reports not-evaluated, never passed: it means no recognised moving alias was found, not that the string is pinned, and never that the weights are.

crosswalk.note: For trained models, MachineLearningStandards owns reproducibility and run configuration. This rule covers only the identifier a deployed system names for a model it did not train.

rules.title: The manifest declares a lifecycle stage
rules.description: The manifest states whether the system is in design, build, evaluation, deployment, monitoring or retirement.
rules.rationale: Several obligations apply only at particular stages, and a system with no declared stage is one where nobody can say which obligations are live.
rules.remediation: Add a lifecycleStage field to the manifest.

rules.title: Retirement is planned before it is needed
rules.description: A retirement plan states how the system is decommissioned and what happens to its data, prompts and traces.
rules.rationale: Retirement is the lifecycle stage most often reached without a plan, and the one where orphaned model access and undeleted personal data outlive the system that justified them.
rules.remediation: Record a retirement plan and reference it from the manifest.

rules.title: The system's safety requirements are stated, or the finding that there are none is recorded
rules.description: A committed safety requirements record names, for each identified hazard, the harm, the safety property the system must hold to prevent it, and the observation that would show the property violated. Where no hazard is identified, the record says so and states how that conclusion was reached.
rules.rationale: A safety property whose violation nobody could observe cannot be shown to have been broken, so it is treated as met by default. And a repository with no record cannot be told apart from one whose team looked carefully and found nothing: the first is missing evidence, the second is a finding.
rules.remediation: Write the record. For each hazard, name the harm, the property, and the observable violation. If none was identified, record that finding and how it was reached rather than leaving silence. No manifest field references the record, so say where it is.

rules.title: Safety requirements and the safety case state the context they hold for, and what ends it
rules.description: The safety requirements record and any safety case state the operating context they hold for — who the system serves, what it is used for, and which effects its outputs can reach — and name the changes to that context or to the system that would make them no longer hold.
rules.rationale: A safety claim with no stated context can meet every counterexample with 'that is not the intended use'. Writing the context down turns that answer into a checkable fact, and naming the invalidating changes is what tells anyone when the case must be revisited.
rules.remediation: State the users, uses and reachable effects the requirements and case assume, including any autonomy tier, tool classification or risk-tier determination the argument relies on, and list the changes that would invalidate them.

rules.title: Every stated safety property is argued in a safety case down to cited evidence
rules.description: Where the safety requirements record states at least one safety property, a committed safety case makes every stated property the subject of a claim, decomposes each claim until every part cites specific evidence, and marks any claim or part that no evidence supports as unsupported rather than omitting it.
rules.rationale: A document that lists reasons to believe a system is safe cannot be disagreed with link by link, and its characteristic failure is the claim nobody could support being quietly left out so the document reads as complete. An argument with marked gaps is honest; one with hidden gaps is not, and reads better.
rules.remediation: Write each stated property as a claim, break it into narrower conditions, cite the evidence for each, and mark every unsupported part explicitly.

rules.title: Safety-case evidence is identified by kind and revision, and is never the argument itself
rules.description: Each citation in a safety case identifies its evidence as a design or configuration fact observable in the repository, a record of an executed test, evaluation or exercise naming the model identifiers, prompt revisions and configuration it ran against, or an assumption about the operating context. No record from a different system revision is cited as current, and no citation is to the case itself, the safety requirements record, or any other statement of intent.
rules.rationale: A document's existence is not evidence that its argument is sound. A case citing the requirement it argues has restated the requirement and called it proof; a case citing an evaluation of the previous model describes a different system; and an assumption listed as evidence is read as though someone observed it.
rules.remediation: Label every citation by kind. For executed records, name the revision they ran against and compare it with the manifest's pinned models. Replace any self-, intent- or stale citation with real evidence, or mark the claim unsupported.

rules.title: The stated safety properties hold while the system runs
rules.description: At inference time, in the operating context the safety case declares, the system keeps every safety property its safety requirements record states.
rules.rationale: This is the requirement the record and the case exist to serve, and the one this framework cannot check. It is stated so that it is visible in every verdict rather than implied by the presence of a case. It is required rather than forbidden because the prohibitive form of AI safety requirements belongs to item 48, Safety and Oversight Prohibitions, which is unwritten.
rules.remediation: Commission evaluation or adversarial exercises against each stated property at the current revision and commit their records. Until a rule can read such records this requirement is reported as not evaluated and must not be read as satisfied; even then, a record establishes behaviour only on the inputs it exercised.
rules.$notEvaluableNote: The subject is model behaviour at inference time, not repository content. A human reading this repository can establish what a safety case argues and whether its citations are real, which lifecycle.safety-evidence-traceable asks; they cannot establish that the running system keeps each stated property, because that is decided by the model, its inputs and its environment during a run. What would make part of it evaluable is a committed record of an executed evaluation or adversarial exercise against the stated properties, from a named harness at a recorded system revision, which a separate rule would check for existence and currency. Even that record establishes behaviour only on the inputs it exercised.
